data.name: GrubTerra

audit.sub: Your own Klaviyo, Appstle and Shopify numbers for the twelve months to September 2026. Twelve of the nineteen live flows were rebuilt on 16 October, so I am checking how the emails are set up, not what they earn. For Michael Servais, by Zee.Media.

wins.title: Build the automated emails you are missing
wins.detail: An automated email is worth 43 cents once the bill-chasing flows come out, a campaign 9.8. Four flows are missing, each priced at the volume of the flow it most resembles in your own account: cart abandonment at checkout abandonment's 7,886 emails, site abandonment at browse abandonment's 18,006, a reorder nudge at the 36,600 the after-delivery series used to send, and a wind-down across the 12,867 people who stopped opening. About 75,000 emails a year at 25 cents, under your own average. The welcome series is priced separately, so it is not in here.

wins.title: Make the welcome series a real series
wins.detail: 11,532 people joined last year and got 1.4 welcome emails each. Your first welcome email earns $1.69. Everything after it earns 24 cents, and there is barely anything after it. Three more each at that same 24 cents is $8,300. The setting change that keeps existing customers out is part of the same job and costs nothing.

wins.title: Put skip and delay inside the pre-charge email
wins.detail: 2,170 cancellations a year at the current rate. Skip, delay and swap buttons inside the single email before a charge turn some of those into skips. It stays one email. Saving 5% is 108 subscriptions, worth two further charges each at your $60.51 average. The 5% is the assumption; the rest is measured.

wins.title: Rebuild the failed-payment sequence
wins.detail: 1,797 people hit a failed charge last year across 31,465 retry attempts, and the flow chasing them is now one email. The old five-email version earned $18,569. Rebuilding it, with a stop rule that works, and recovering three points more of those people is 54 subscriptions worth two charges each at $60.51.

wins.title: Separate the renewals from what email earned
wins.detail: Shopify and Klaviyo agree on September to the dollar, so nothing is missing. But over half this store renews itself: $309,936 of $580,945, and 5,120 of 9,452 orders, across the six months the account has held a renewal record. Taking out the six bill-chasing flows turns the credited number into one worth deciding from.

wins.title: Test every automated email, and keep testing
wins.detail: Every email that leaves your automated set untested is a visit you only get once. 131,945 of them went last year once the bill-chasing flows come out, earning $56,934, and 24 tests sit built and switched off. Three subject line tests a week and three design tests, each one recorded, lift what every one of those emails earns. At 10% that is $5,700 a year, on emails you already send, which none of the wins above touch.

audit.title: Account audit

findings.body:
Shopify and Klaviyo both put September at $113,503. Placed Order matches to the dollar, so nothing is missing. What that credit sits on is a longer answer, three cards down.

CHECKOUT10 and CHECKOUT20 have issued 32 unique codes since 19 October, the most recent this morning. GRUB5 and GRUB25 are typed as plain text into checkout abandonment, so they live in Shopify where a Klaviyo key cannot see them.

CREDIT is the one worth a minute. The win-back flow waits 35 days and only went live on 16 October, so nobody has reached the first email and the coupon has never been called. Four of its eight versions print “$7.73” into the subject line. Check it on the Coupons screen before it starts sending.

tldr.do: Search CREDIT on the Coupons screen before 20 November, which is when that flow first sends.
tldr.what: Your tracking is accurate to the dollar. Two discount codes work, the third has never been handed out.

chart.note: Every one of the eight calls CREDIT, and five print the $7.73 into the subject line. Open any message to see it. Checking the coupon once settles all eight.

groups.title: Email 1, day 35

groups.note: three versions in a split test

findings.title: What you asked: your numbers are right, and two codes of three are fine

findings.body:
Twelve flows went off on 16 October and twelve went live the same day, five more by the 30th. Nothing has run long enough to judge on what it earns yet.

What the first fifteen days show. Fifteen days either side, the same flows sent 7,729 emails earning $2,518, then 4,280 earning $1,308. That is $1,210 a fortnight behind, about $31,000 a year if it holds. A new flow does take weeks to fill, and the welcome series genuinely improved.

What will not recover on its own is the two flows switched off with nothing behind them. The after-delivery series was earning $798 a fortnight when it went. The rest of this audit is which parts to put back and what that is worth: $52,400 a year.

tldr.do: Put back the after-delivery series first. It was earning $798 a fortnight on the day it was turned off.
tldr.what: On 16 October twelve flows were switched off and twelve new ones went live. Two were never replaced, and the set is running about $1,200 a fortnight behind.

chart.note: Each row opens the flow doing that job today. Two of the subscription flows were swapped again in the last week of October, so the clock on measuring either build has restarted.

findings.title: Your whole automated set was rebuilt in a day, and it is sending half as much

findings.body:
This did not start in October. Against its own past: the store did $493,868 in the six months to March and $580,945 in the six to September, up 17.6%. Email went from $143,235 to $156,723, up 9.4%, on 29% more mail.

Revenue per email delivered fell from 13.3 cents to 11.3 across those two halves. Growth bought with volume, not value, and it stops the moment capture flattens.

Email and SMS are credited with $309,650 of a $1,074,807 store over twelve months, which is 28.8%. That is a healthy number on its face. The next card is what it is sitting on.

tldr.do: Grow by making each email earn more. More volume on this list is the expensive way to the same number.
tldr.what: Email is credited with 28.8% of the store, but the growth came from sending more, not from earning more per email.

chart.note: Email and SMS as a share of the store Klaviyo tracks, month by month, to the last complete month. Bars at the base show what was actually sent to earn it. The 28.8% in the text is the twelve months to September, which is the window this audit measures.
Emails delivered rose from 1,076,923 to 1,389,239 across the same two halves, and revenue per email delivered fell from 13.3 cents to 11.3.

findings.title: The store grew 18%. You sent 29% more email to grow 9%.

findings.body:
No Klaviyo event records an Appstle charge with a dollar on it. The only renewal record in the account is Subscription Recurring Order, fed by your Upstack tracking, from April. Six months is the window. In it the store did $580,945 and $309,936 of that was renewals, across 5,120 of its 9,452 orders. Email and SMS are credited with $165,076.

On top of that, $20,885 of last year's flow revenue came from six flows whose only job is to chase a bill already due: failed payment, payment resumed, paused, reactivation, new subscription, address updated. Strip them and email's share of the store is 26.9% rather than 28.8%.

It is the number we would both be judged on, so worth agreeing on it now.

tldr.do: When you judge what email earns, leave out the six flows that only chase a bill already due.
tldr.what: $309,936 of a $580,945 store is recurring subscription charges. Some of what email is credited with was always going to happen.

chart.note: The only renewal record in the account, from April. Its 5,238 raw events hold 118 repeats, taken out. That feed puts the whole store at $578,177, within half a percent of the figure beside it.

findings.title: Over half this store renews itself, so read the credit carefully

findings.body:
The Appstle event this flow waits for recorded nothing at all from November 2025 to September 2026, then 1,070 in October. No Klaviyo flow warned anybody before their card was charged until last month.

The first version went live in the rebuild, delivered 480 emails, and was switched off on the 29th. The one live now went up on the 28th and has delivered 184. They overlapped for a day and ran alone either side of it, so neither has a clean measurement.

The live version holds two sends. One notice before a charge is the right number: every extra reminder is another invitation to reconsider. Put the work inside that one email: charge date, amount, what is in the box, and buttons to skip, delay or swap.

tldr.do: Keep it to one email before the charge, and put skip, delay and swap buttons inside it.
tldr.what: Until October no Klaviyo email warned anybody before their card was charged. The flow doing it now is two weeks old.

chart.leak: 2,427 active subscribers, about 850 charges a month at a $60.51 average order value. It's the one email that decides whether a renewal happens.

findings.title: The pre-charge email is the one that decides a renewal

findings.body:
The flow that handled failed charges was the account's highest earner: $18,569 from 47,776 emails. On 29 October, in the same fortnight of switching, it went to draft and Failed Payment Flow Michael replaced it. The live flow is one email after a delay. The one it replaced was five emails with three tests inside it.

That is thin cover. 1,797 people hit a failed charge last year across 31,465 retry events, because Appstle retries hard.

A trap is waiting in the old build. Its exit was “Transaction Success Event from Appstle zero times since starting this flow”. The intent was right, but that event has fired zero times in twelve months, so nobody was let out early. Stop the emails when the customer's next successful order is recorded.

tldr.do: Rebuild the sequence. Don't copy the old rule for when to stop emailing someone, because it never worked.
tldr.what: The five-email sequence that chased failed payments earned $18,569. It is switched off, and one email replaced it.

chart.note: The exit the old build waited on has fired zero times in twelve months. Whatever is rebuilt has to stop on the next successful order instead.

items.label: People who hit a failed charge

findings.title: Your best-earning flow was replaced by a single email

findings.body:
Through last winter, cancellations ran at three to ten times new subscriptions: January lost 553 against 54 started. In April it reversed and has stayed reversed for six months: 888 started against 2,417 cancelled in the first half, 1,725 against 1,085 in the second.

The email setup does not explain that reversal, and here is what I mean. Until October nobody got a warning before their card was charged. The flow chasing failed payments could never tell it had worked, so it kept emailing people who had already paid. The subscription welcome was one thin flow. Every email that normally keeps somebody subscribed was missing or broken.

A swing this large with nothing driving it is usually a change in how cancellations get recorded. So what changed in April?

tldr.do: Tell us what changed in April before either of us books this as a win.
tldr.what: Cancellations outran new subscriptions three to one last winter. Since April that has reversed, and no email explains it.

chart.note: Counted as subscription events rather than people. Both series are on the same scale, so the crossing in April is real and not a trick of the axes.

findings.title: Churn turned around in April, and I want to know why before we bank it

findings.body:
11,532 people subscribed over twelve months and 6,989 arrived in the last three. July, August and September brought 2,007, 3,004 and 1,978. That is a change of gear, and it fits the Meta spend you described.

The list has not soured for it. 6,262 unsubscribed out of 2,548,640 emails, which is 0.246%, and 0.015% marked you as spam, a rate that has roughly halved. The segmentation underneath is better than most accounts I audit.

All 24 forms in Klaviyo are drafts. Everybody joins through Alia, which we cannot see into, so your offer and your pop-up are the one part of this account I cannot audit.

So more people than ever are arriving. What they arrive into is the next two cards.

tldr.do: Nothing to fix here. It is the reason the two cards after this one matter.
tldr.what: 11,532 people joined in a year and 6,989 of them in the last three months, with unsubscribes and complaints flat.

chart.note: Bars are new email subscribers each month. The shaded area is the unsubscribe rate and the dashed line is spam complaints. Intake trebled from July and the unsubscribe rate followed it only as far as 0.30%.

findings.title: Your acquisition is working better than it ever has

findings.body:
The welcome series triggers when someone joins the master email list, and its only filter is “Placed Order zero times since starting this flow”.

That phrase asks whether they've ordered since they entered, not whether they've ever ordered. So a customer who has bought from you ten times, and who signs up through a popup or gets added by Alia, drops into the new-customer welcome and is offered a first-order discount they don't need.

Changing it to “over all time” takes about thirty seconds. Length is the other thing: 15,943 emails to 11,532 new subscribers, about 1.4 each. Your first welcome email earns $1.69. The ones after it earn 24 cents, and there are few of them.

tldr.do: One setting: check whether they have ever ordered, not just since they joined. Thirty seconds.
tldr.what: Your welcome emails go to people who have already bought from you ten times, and offer them a first-order discount.

chart.note: 1.4 emails per new subscriber. The first one earns $1.69; everything after it earns 24 cents.

findings.title: Your welcome series lets existing customers in

findings.body:
The win-back flow and the pre-delivery upsell already exclude anyone tagged as an active Appstle subscriber. The three retargeting flows don't: browse abandonment, checkout abandonment and the Peck Purity checkout flow.

Two costs. They get reminded, with a discount attached, about something they already pay for monthly, which invites them to look at what they are spending. And when the scheduled charge goes through afterwards, Klaviyo books it as a conversion that flow didn't earn.

Worth saying the Peck Purity split itself is clean: both flows fire on the same event, but their product rules send each customer down one of the two, not both.

tldr.do: Add the same skip-active-subscribers rule your win-back flow already has to all three.
tldr.what: Three flows will email somebody a discount on the product they already get delivered on subscription.

chart.note: The filter already exists in this account. It just hasn't been applied everywhere it belongs.

findings.title: Three retargeting flows still email your subscribers

findings.body:
Flows delivered 188,824 emails for $77,819. Campaigns delivered 2,277,338 for $222,138. Take out the $20,885 that only chased bills, 56,879 emails of it, and an automated email is worth 43 cents against 9.8 for a campaign email. Automated email is 7.7% of everything you send, and 5.5% once those billing flows come out of it too.

This is not an argument against campaigns. 199 a year plus 30 SMS sends is about right for a list this size, and your unsubscribe rate says people are not sick of hearing from you.

It's an argument about where the next hour of work goes. Checkout abandonment earns $1.36 an email and sent 7,085 all year. The welcome series earns 64 cents an email and sent 15,943 of them.

tldr.do: Build the automated emails you are missing, so more of your sending is the kind that earns four times as much. Campaigns carry on as they are.
tldr.what: An automated email earns 43 cents. A campaign earns 9.8. Only 7.7% of what you send is automated at all.

chart.note: Both series are dollars on the same scale. The line is 7.7% of the volume and about a quarter of the money.
Both the revenue and the email count here exclude the six flows that only chase a bill already due: $20,885 across 56,879 emails.
chart.metricLabel: Cents per email delivered, billing flows stripped

findings.title: A campaign email earns 10 cents. An automated email earns 43.

findings.body:
Nineteen flows are live and acquisition and shipping are well covered. Retention is where the gaps are.

There's checkout abandonment but no cart abandonment, and they are different moments: one catches the people who reached payment, the other the much larger group who added to cart and left. No site abandonment either, no way of winding down people who stopped opening, despite 12,867 people sitting in a segment built for one, and nothing that nudges a first-time buyer to order again.

The after-delivery series belongs on this list too until it is put back. And the three shipping flows are 17% of your flow volume at 16 cents an email, untested.

tldr.do: After the after-delivery series is back, build these, starting with the reorder nudge. People feeding flocks run out on a schedule.
tldr.what: Four standard flows are missing: cart abandonment, site abandonment, a wind-down for people who stopped opening, and a reorder nudge.

chart.note: Measured against the retention framework we build for every client in this category.

findings.title: What isn't built

findings.body:
Two tests built in the rebuild point their main button at GrubTerra Fresh Black Soldier Fly Larvae for Reptiles. Not the dried five-pound bag for chickens.

One sits in the welcome series, on the branch for people who told your quiz they want more eggs. The button reads “Grab your first bag of Grub Larvae with 20% off” and goes to the reptile page. The other is in browse abandonment.

Nobody has landed there yet: neither test has been switched on, and the original version of each is correct. The moment either starts, half the traffic through your best acquisition branch hits the wrong product, and the automatic winner selection reads those clicks as a verdict on the copy.

tldr.do: Fix both links before those tests start, or half your best new customers land on the wrong product.
tldr.what: Two tests point their main button at the live reptile grubs instead of the dried bag for chickens.

chart.leak: Product links only, not every button in every email, so this is a floor rather than a clean bill of health.

stages.label: A/B variants checked against their control (64)
Pointing somewhere the control does not (4)

findings.title: Two tests are pointed at the wrong product

findings.body:
This account is not untested. Across your automated emails there are 40 A/B tests built and 12 have already run to a winner. That is more of a testing habit than most accounts I audit.

The problem is the ones that never started. Four are running today. Twenty-four are built, split fifty-fifty, set to pick a winner on their own, and have never been switched on.

A test that never runs earns nothing, teaches nothing and goes off: all 24 were written against the emails as they stood on the day of the rebuild, and two point at the wrong product.

tldr.do: Switch them on or delete them. They were written for emails that have since changed.
tldr.what: Twenty-four A/B tests are built and ready to go but have never been switched on. Four are running.

chart.themSub: tests running today, out of 40 built across 19 live flows
chart.footTail: against the twelve this account has concluded in total, each one a gain your automated emails keep.

findings.title: Forty tests are built. Four are running.

findings.body:
The first fortnight is wiring, not a redesign. Put the after-delivery series back, because it was earning $798 a fortnight the day it went. Change one word in the welcome series filter. Fix the two wrong-product links before any dormant test starts. Rebuild the full sequence on the failed-payment flow, with a stop rule that works. Settle which upcoming-order flow is the one. Confirm the win-back coupon before it first sends in November. Put the subscriber exclusion on browse abandonment, checkout abandonment and Peck Purity.

After that we begin a regular testing schedule inside the automated emails: three subject line tests a week, three design overhauls, three new messages.

The six wins above come to $52,400 a year, each priced off your own numbers. Most of our clients sit between $3M and $20M. Pricing is public.

tldr.do: Start with the after-delivery series, then the welcome series filter. Both are same-day jobs.
tldr.what: The first fortnight restores missing emails and fixes settings and product links. No redesign, all of it measurable inside a month.
